meta.title: Ethnic name pools for a gladiator ludus game
meta.keyPrinciple: Almost no gladiator fought under his birth name. Gladiators were slaves, war captives or auctorati, and the epigraphic record shows them bearing a single Latin or Greek ARENA name regardless of origin (Flamma, the best-documented gladiator, is recorded as natione Syrus). Generate a birth name from a group's pool, then assign an arena name from arenaNames on enrolment.
meta.armatureWarning: Thraex, Gallus and Samnis are fighting styles named after long-defeated peoples, not ethnicities. Do not couple armature to origin in the generator.

confidence.A: attested for that people in the ancient record
confidence.R: plausible reconstruction from attested name-elements; not itself on record

thracian.label: Thracian
thracian.convention: single name, no family name; short simple names and dithematic compounds
notes: Patronymic by apposition in the Greek genitive: Mucakenthos Beithyos, 'son of Bithus'.
Romanised Thracians keep the native name as cognomen: Aurelius Mucatralis, Traianus Mucianus.
Do not append Latin -us to the compounds. Mucaporis is right; Mucaporius is not.
Sparatocus is the Odrysian royal name behind Spartacus, our one genuinely Thracian gladiator.
Dynastic names are status-loaded; sparing use for slaves.

gallic.label: Gallic
gallic.convention: single name, often a dithematic compound of heroic vocabulary; under Rome kept as cognomen
notes: -rix means 'king'. Keep it under roughly 15% of Gallic output or it reads as parody.
Both raw Gaulish and Latinised forms are legitimate: Segomaros / Segomarus.
The Gallus armature was obsolete by the early Empire, replaced by the murmillo; the Ludus Gallicus in Rome is nevertheless real.
Do not use Insular Celtic names (Conall, Fergus, Brian, Niall) - wrong branch, centuries too late.

roman.label: Roman
roman.convention: gladiators bore a single arena name; freeborn volunteers could keep the full citizen formula

birthNames.note: Roman gladiators have no separate birth-name pool - they draw directly from arenaNames. For free volunteers and citizens, build a full name from lanistae.triaNomina.

notes: A suffix in -ianus after an arena name marks the owning school, not the name: Hilarus Neronianus = 'Hilarus of the Neronian ludus'. Good mechanic to model on purchase.
Greek and Latin forms interchange freely: Neikephoros / Nicephorus, Hermas / Herma.
Freeborn auctorati may appear under a full tria nomina with the arena name as cognomen.

numidian.label: Numidian
numidian.convention: single Libyco-Berber name; Punic names circulate alongside native Libyan ones
numidian.recordDepth: thin - script only partly deciphered, several readings contested

compoundGenerator.warning: Reconstruction only. Keep a minority of output.

notes: -bal endings invoke the Punic god Baal; more likely in Carthaginianised families than purely Libyan ones.
Tacfarinas is the standout: native in form, non-royal in status, exactly the profile that ends in an arena.
Romanised Africans carry the Libyan name as cognomen: Lucius Iulius Iugurtha.
Avoid modern Amazigh given names (Idir, Yidir) - anachronistic by two millennia.

germanic.label: Germanic
germanic.convention: single dithematic name; every form we have is filtered through Latin
notes: Chronology matters most here. Alaric, Genseric, Theodoric, Athanaric, Fritigern are 3rd-5th century; wrong for a 1st-2nd century ludus.
Chrauttius and Gambax come from the Vindolanda tablets - ordinary soldiers, not princes.
Germanic captives genuinely reached the arena in volume under Caesar, Augustus, Nero and Domitian.
Do not use Norse names (Ragnar, Bjorn, Sigurd, Leif) - wrong branch, eight centuries early.

nubian.label: Nubian / sub-Saharan African
nubian.convention: single Meroitic name; the record is Kushite, not gladiatorial
nubian.recordDepth: very thin - and zero named gladiators of this origin exist
nubian.honestCaveat: No gladiator is attested as Nubian or sub-Saharan African by name. Not one. Romans knew Nubia, fought it under Augustus and enslaved people from it, and Aethiopes appear in art and in the venationes - but no named arena fighter. Everything below is Kushite onomastics, not arena evidence.

compoundGenerator.warning: Amani- names are overwhelmingly ROYAL (the god Amun). Naming an enslaved fighter Amanideqo is like calling a galley-slave 'Prince Augustus'. For rank-and-file use the commoner shapes: two or three syllables, -a and -u endings, no god element.

recommendedApproach.note: Memnon especially - the Ethiopian king of the Trojan cycle, exactly the literary joke a lanista would make. Pair a Latin arena name with an origin tag and surface the Meroitic birth name as flavour only.

syrian.label: Syrian / Levantine
syrian.convention: single Aramaic name, often theophoric, with a bar- patronymic in Palmyrene usage
syrian.recordDepth: good - the Palmyrene corpus is large
syrian.anchor: Flamma, the best-documented gladiator in the Latin record, is natione Syrus (CIL X 7297, Lilybaeum).
notes: Greek and Latin renderings diverge hard: Wahballat -> Vaballathus, Odainat -> Odaenathus, Bat Zabbai -> Zenobia. Free texture for a Romanisation mechanic.
After AD 70 Titus distributed Judaean captives to provincial amphitheatres - one of the best-evidenced origin stories available.
Palmyrene tombstones carry three- and four-generation patronymic chains; good for a wealthy Syrian patron.
Syrian archers were a famous auxiliary speciality - a defensible characterisation.

greek.label: Greek
greek.convention: single name; the richest gladiatorial pool of all, from Greek-East relief stelae
notes: Greek-East monuments record rank by palus (primus to octavus palus) and crown-count, not a simple win tally - a ready-made historical rank system.
Latin names appear freely among Greek-East gladiators and Greek names freely in the West. Do not partition the pools strictly.
In Greek inscriptions gladiators are monomachoi; the patron of games is a priest of the imperial cult (archiereus / asiarch), not a lanista.
Greek names are also the standard stock of freedmen - a good default for the ludus doctor and medicus.
Avoid modern Greek forms (Yannis, Kostas, Dimitris).

arenaNames.note: Assign on enrolment, regardless of the fighter's origin. This is how the record actually looks.

attestedGladiators.name: Flamma
attestedGladiators.note: CIL X 7297; natione Syrus, 34 fights, 21 wins

ludusSuffixes.note: Appended to an arena name to mark the owning school; generate from the ludus name, not stored with the fighter.

attested.name: Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus Batiatus
attested.note: Spartacus broke away from his school

attested.name: Gaius Aurelius Scaurus
attested.note: Valerius Maximus 2.3.2 - Rutilius Rufus borrowed his trainers for the legions in 105 BC; not literally called lanista in the text

attested.name: Aulus Suettius Anteros
attested.note: freedman-style name: Latin praenomen + nomen + Greek cognomen

freedmanCognomina.note: The most authentic lanista profile: the trade was infamis, so many lanistae were freedmen. Formula = Latin praenomen + former owner's nomen + own Greek slave name as cognomen.

notes: A lanista was legally infamis, ranked with pimps and barred from civic honour - which is why so few are named.
The editor who pays for a show is a magistrate buying popularity; the lanista is the despised tradesman who supplies the men. Two different social positions.
Women could own gladiatorial familiae and finance games - Eumachia of Pompeii is the model.
Imperial ludi in Rome were state property run by an equestrian procurator familiae gladiatoriae, not a private lanista.

attested.name: Ludus Magnus
attested.note: the great school, tunnel-linked to the Colosseum

attested.name: Ludus Matutinus
attested.note: 'the morning school' - trained bestiarii for the beast-hunts

attested.name: Ludus Aemilius
attested.note: older; later converted into the balneum Polycleti

attested.name: Ludus Iulianus
attested.note: gladiators appear as 'Iulianus'; Caesar kept a large ludus at Capua and the name passes to the imperial house

attested.name: familia gladiatoria Cn. Allei Nigidi Mai
school of Cn. Cornelius Lentulus Batiatus

ownerPattern.rule: Take the owner's nomen, drop -ius, add -ianus. Cornelius -> Ludus Cornelianus.
ownerPattern.alternate: Familia gladiatoria + owner's full name in the genitive, e.g. 'Familia gladiatoria M. Vetti Diadumeni'.

ethnicOrFunctionPattern.rule: A third genuine pattern - Dacicus, Gallicus and Matutinus all exist.

recordDepthSummary.greek: excellent - use freely, all attested for gladiators
recordDepthSummary.thracian: very good - large onomastic corpus, compounds generate well
recordDepthSummary.gallic: very good - Caesar plus craftsmen's names; throttle -rix
recordDepthSummary.germanic: moderate - elite-skewed and Latin-filtered; watch chronology
recordDepthSummary.numidian: thin - script partly undeciphered; supplement with Punic and flag uncertainty
recordDepthSummary.nubian: very thin, and zero named gladiators - use the origin-tag plus arena-name approach
